requirements: The core contributions of PM-KVQ (Progressive Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for long-CoT LLMs) have been reproduced, including progressive quantization with Equivalent Right Shift, block-wise memory allocation via Integer Programming, calibration with positional interpolation, and the reported reasoning-benchmark accuracy and throughput results on 7B–70B DeepSeek-R1-Distill / QwQ models.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware (8×A100-80G server; 1×RTX 4090-24G, 1×A100-40G, 1×A100-80G target GPUs), CUDA/PyTorch stack, KIVI inference engine and CUDA kernels (2/4-bit plus new 8/16-bit and bit-width-shrinking kernels), CVXPY solver, and OpenCompass evaluation harness needed for PM-KVQ are installed and callable.
Hardware inventory and target-GPU mapping used across PM-KVQ experiments are provisioned and correctly assigned per model size.

Code has been implemented that detects and requires an 8×A100-80G GPU server for the fake-quantization accuracy runs described in Section 4.1.3, exposing a check that fails with a clear error when fewer than 8 A100-80G devices are visible.

A target-GPU mapping is implemented that assigns 1×RTX 4090-24G to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, 1×A100-40G to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and 1×A100-80G to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B and QwQ-32B, matching the Target GPU column of Table 2.

Code has been implemented that queries the available GPU memory before an experiment starts and validates it against the memory required by the batch-size / bit-width configuration for the assigned target GPU, aborting with a diagnostic if the request exceeds capacity.
The CUDA-enabled PyTorch stack required by PM-KVQ and its BF16 KV Cache pipeline is installed and functional.

A PyTorch build with CUDA support is installed and imports cleanly; torch.cuda.is_available() returns True and the CUDA runtime version reported is compatible with the A100 (SM 8.0) and RTX 4090 (SM 8.9) target devices.

Code has been implemented that allocates BF16 tensors on GPU and performs matmul/attention primitives, confirming that all model weights and un-quantized KV entries can be held in BF16 as required by Section 4.1.2.

The KIVI inference engine and its extended CUDA kernel suite (original 2/4-bit kernels plus new 8-bit, 16-bit, and bit-width-shrinking kernels) are installed, callable from Python, and numerically correct.

The KIVI inference engine (Liu et al., 2024c) is vendored or installed as a dependency, importable from the reproduction package, and its per-channel Key / per-token Value asymmetric group-wise quantization (group size 128) can be invoked on a sample KV Cache tensor.

The original KIVI 2-bit and 4-bit CUDA kernels for KV Cache dequantization and attention are compiled successfully against the installed CUDA toolkit and produce non-error outputs when invoked on GPU tensors.

A new 8-bit CUDA kernel (for storing/reading KV Cache at 8-bit as needed by the progressive-quantization intermediate stage) has been implemented alongside the KIVI 2/4-bit kernels and is callable through the same interface.

A new 16-bit CUDA kernel (for storing KV Cache in the initial BF16/INT16 stage of progressive quantization) has been implemented and integrated so decoding can consume 16-bit KV entries with the same op interface as the KIVI quantized kernels.

A bit-width shrinking CUDA kernel that converts a stored KV Cache buffer from 2b-bit to b-bit in place (for b ∈ {8,4,2}) using the Equivalent Right Shift formulation of Section 3.1 has been implemented and is invocable during decoding.

The bit-width shrinking kernel is numerically equivalent (bit-exact for the integer codes and matching within floating-point rounding for the dequantized values) to first dequantizing the 2b-bit KV Cache to BF16 and then re-quantizing it to b-bit, as required by Theorem D.1.
The CVXPY-based solver for the block-wise bit-width Integer Programming problem is installed and usable within the pipeline.

CVXPY (Diamond & Boyd, 2016) is installed as a dependency, imports cleanly, and at least one MIP-capable backend solver (e.g. GLPK_MI / CBC / SCIP) is available so the Integer Programming problem in Section 3.2 can be dispatched.

A smoke test formulates the Section 3.2 block-wise bit-width allocation as a CVXPY Integer Program (with the per-block one-hot variables x_{i,b} and the memory-budget constraint) and solves it to optimality end-to-end without raising SolverError.
For every model size used in Table 2 (7B–70B), the CVXPY solve for the block-wise bit-width Integer Program completes within a few seconds on CPU, as claimed at the end of Section 3.2.

The IFEval task configuration in OpenCompass reports all four metrics used in Table 6 — Prompt Strict, Prompt Loose, Instruct Strict, and Instruct Loose — for a supplied set of model responses.

Progressive KV Cache quantization is implemented: KV Cache is stored in 16-bit initially and bit-width is shrunk 16→8→4→2 once memory is saturated, using the Equivalent Right Shift transform with Sb=(2^b+1)·S_{2b}, Zb=Z_{2b}, and mathematical equivalence (Theorem D.1) demonstrable in code; the paper's INT16 handling of the first token and 128-token sliding window is preserved.

The progressive storage lifecycle of the KV Cache — initial 16-bit storage, bit-width shrinking cadence, per-block Fbit configuration, and memory-budget bookkeeping — is implemented as described in Section 3.1.

Code has been implemented so that at the start of generation the KV Cache for every transformer block is stored in 16-bit precision (BF16 or INT16 container) regardless of the block's configured final bit-width (Fbit).

Code has been implemented so that the progressive bit-width shrinking schedule uses powers of two, monotonically decreasing in the order 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 bits, and does not permit non-power-of-two intermediate steps.

The bit-width shrinking operation for a transformer block is triggered only when its per-block memory budget for the KV Cache is fully occupied by the current 2b-bit storage; no shrinking is performed while spare memory remains.
The final bit-width Fbit (the target bit-width after all shrinking) is configurable per transformer block, supporting values 2, 4, and 8 as used in the paper's experiments.

Code has been implemented to compute each block's KV Cache memory budget from the model's maximum context length, per-token KV element count (heads × head_dim × 2), and the block's Fbit, and to use this budget to decide when shrinking is invoked.

The progressive quantization state (current bit-width, remaining budget, shrinking history) is tracked independently per transformer block so that blocks assigned different Fbits progress on independent shrinking schedules.

The Equivalent Right Shift (ERS) transform, which shrinks a group-wise asymmetric 2b-bit quantized KV tensor to b-bit while remaining mathematically equivalent to dequant-then-requant (Theorem D.1), is implemented for the transitions 16→8, 8→4, and 4→2 bits.
Code has been implemented to update the scaling factor when shrinking from 2b-bit to b-bit as Sb = (2^b + 1) · S_{2b}, matching Equation (3) and Section 3.1 exactly.
Code has been implemented so that the zero point is preserved during Equivalent Right Shift: Zb = Z_{2b} (the zero point is not modified by the shrinking step).

The integer bit-shrinking operation performs a right-shift of the 2b-bit integer tensor by b bits (equivalently integer division by 2^b + 1 with the ERS rounding rule) rather than a floating-point dequant-requant round-trip.

Code has been implemented to shrink a group-wise asymmetric 16-bit KV Cache tensor to 8-bit via the Equivalent Right Shift transform, producing correctly typed 8-bit integers and updated (S_8, Z_8) scales.
Code has been implemented to shrink an 8-bit KV Cache tensor to 4-bit via the Equivalent Right Shift transform, producing correctly typed 4-bit integers and updated (S_4, Z_4) scales.
Code has been implemented to shrink a 4-bit KV Cache tensor to 2-bit via the Equivalent Right Shift transform, producing correctly typed 2-bit integers and updated (S_2, Z_2) scales.

The quantization used inside the progressive KV Cache pipeline is asymmetric group-wise quantization with group size 128, matching Section 4.1.3, and this grouping is preserved across every ERS shrinking step.

On a random BF16 tensor, the ERS transform Q_b(X_BF16) is numerically identical (elementwise equal within integer arithmetic tolerance) to the reference pipeline that dequantizes X_{2b} back to floating point and then re-quantizes to b bits, confirming Theorem D.1 as claimed in Section 3.1 and Appendix D.
The Equivalent Right Shift transform is applied uniformly to both Key Cache and Value Cache tensors within each block, with the same Sb/Zb formulas and shift operation used for both.

The rounding behavior of the ERS shift correctly handles both remainder cases from the Appendix D proof — 0 ≤ r ≤ 2^{b-1} (rounds down to q) and 2^{b-1}+1 ≤ r ≤ 2^b (rounds up to q+1) — with no off-by-one errors at the boundary.

After ERS, the effective quantization range S_b · (2^b − 1) reproduces the dynamic range of the 2b-bit tensor S_{2b} · (2^{2b} − 1) up to the ratio (2^b + 1) / (2^{2b} − 1), so the compressed cache still spans the original data range.
The first-token INT16 preservation and 128-token INT16 sliding window inherited from KIVI/SKVQ (Section 4.1.2) are implemented and correctly interact with progressive shrinking.
Code has been implemented so that the Key and Value pair corresponding to the first generated/prompt token is always stored in INT16 and is never shrunk to a lower bit-width.
Code has been implemented for a 128-token recent-token sliding window whose KV entries are stored in INT16 during decoding, matching the SKVQ-style window used in the paper.

The sliding window advances by one token per decoding step: as a new token is appended in INT16, the token evicted from the trailing edge of the window becomes eligible for progressive quantization/shrinking.
When bit-width shrinking events fire, the first-token INT16 KV entry is skipped by the shrink kernel and remains INT16 after every 16→8, 8→4, and 4→2 transition of the surrounding cache.
Only KV entries outside the {first token} ∪ {last 128 tokens} set are eligible for progressive shrinking; entries inside these regions are excluded from ERS on every decoding step.

Progressive quantization is integrated into the decoding loop so it operates step-by-step, is inexpensive when idle, and delivers the cumulative-error reduction Section 3.1 advertises versus uniform-Fbit quantization.

Code has been implemented so that on every decoding step the KV of the new token is appended in 16-bit and, in the same step, any block whose memory has just saturated triggers exactly one ERS shrinking pass on the eligible region of its cache.

When memory is not saturated, the decoding-step hook for progressive quantization is a no-op (no shrinking, no dequant-requant, no scale/zero-point rewrite), consistent with the Section 4.3 claim that shrinking overhead is negligible.

In a controlled decode of ≥32K tokens, the mean squared quantization error of the KV Cache under progressive quantization (Fbit=2 with 16-bit initial storage) is strictly lower than the error under uniform 2-bit quantization applied at every step, reproducing the cumulative-error-reduction argument of Section 3.1.

The decoding loop supports per-transformer-block Fbit as produced by the Section 3.2 memory allocator: two blocks with different Fbits progress along distinct shrinking schedules within the same decode.
The progressive quantization module exposes an interface that consumes the per-block Fbit assignment from the Section 3.2 block-wise memory allocator without hard-coding a uniform Fbit.
The public API and configuration surface for progressive quantization exposes the necessary knobs (per-block Fbit, bit-width set) and emits observable logs of shrinking events.
The KV Cache quantizer's public API accepts an Fbit value (or per-block Fbit vector) as an argument and routes it through to the progressive shrinking scheduler.

Configuration validation rejects Fbit values outside the paper's supported optional bit set (B = {4,8} for the 4-bit setting; B = {2,4} for the 2-bit setting) with an explicit error, matching Section 4.1.3.

Every bit-width shrinking event is logged with at least the transformer block index, the old bit-width, the new bit-width, and the decoding step at which it fired, providing an observable trace of the progressive schedule.
Deterministic unit tests exist for the Section 3.1 core primitives so that regressions in the Equivalent Right Shift, shrinking trigger, and INT16 preservation logic are caught locally.

A deterministic unit test constructs a known BF16 tensor, computes X_{2b} then applies ERS to obtain X_b, computes the reference dequant-requant b-bit result, and asserts elementwise equality (per Theorem D.1) for at least b ∈ {8,4,2}.
A deterministic unit test asserts that the ERS module returns S_b == (2^b + 1) * S_{2b} and Z_b == Z_{2b} on a synthetic input group.

A deterministic unit test drives a fake decoding loop that fills the KV Cache to the memory budget and asserts that a shrinking event fires exactly at the step where the budget is first exceeded, and not before.

A deterministic unit test verifies that after multiple shrinking events the first-token KV entry remains INT16 and the last 128 KV entries also remain INT16, while all other entries have been shrunk to Fbit.

The per-block Taylor-based sensitivity metric s_{i,b} for both K and V caches is computed on the calibration set; the Integer Programming problem is formulated with the correct objective, memory-budget constraint, one-hot bit selection, and optional bit-widths B={4,8} for LLaMA-8B and B={2,4} for others; CVXPY solves it within seconds and produces the reported per-block Fbit assignments.
The first-order Taylor sensitivity metric for the KV Cache in each transformer block is computed correctly on the calibration dataset.

Code has been implemented that computes the Key Cache sensitivity term for the i-th transformer block as (Q_b(K_i) - K_i) ⊙ G_{K_i}, matching the first-order Taylor approximation described in Equation (5) of Section 3.2.
Code has been implemented that computes the Value Cache sensitivity term (Q_b(V_i) - V_i) ⊙ G_{V_i} with an analogous formula to the Key Cache sensitivity.

Code has been implemented that aggregates the per-block sensitivity s_{i,b} for both K and V caches as the sum of the absolute (or squared) Taylor terms over all elements, producing a scalar per (block i, bit-width b) pair as in Equation (6).

Code has been implemented that runs a forward+backward pass on the arXiv-RedPajama calibration set to compute the loss L and back-propagates to obtain the gradients G_{K_i} and G_{V_i} of L with respect to each block's Key and Value cache.
The quantization error term Q_b(K_i) - K_i uses the same asymmetric group-wise quantizer with group size 128 defined in Equation (1) so sensitivity numbers reflect the actual runtime quantizer.

Code has been implemented that iterates over every candidate bit-width b in the optional set B and every transformer block i, populating an N×|B| sensitivity table s_{i,b} used as input to the Integer Programming solver.

When run end-to-end on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, the produced sensitivity values are strictly positive, finite, and monotonically increase as the candidate bit-width b decreases within B (2-bit sensitivity ≥ 4-bit sensitivity ≥ 8-bit sensitivity).
The block-wise bit-width allocation is formulated as the Integer Programming problem stated in Section 3.2 with the correct objective, constraints, and decision variables.
Code has been implemented that constructs the objective function as the double sum over blocks i and bit-widths b of s_{i,b} · x_{i,b}, to be minimized.

Code has been implemented that enforces the memory-budget constraint sum_{i,b} Mem(b) · x_{i,b} ≤ M, where Mem(b) is the per-block quantized KV Cache memory at bit-width b and M is the total memory budget for KV Cache across all transformer blocks.
Code has been implemented that enforces the one-hot constraint sum_b x_{i,b} = 1 for every transformer block i so exactly one bit-width is selected per block.
Code has been implemented that declares the decision variables x_{i,b} as binary (integer in {0,1}) so the resulting solve is a true Integer Program rather than an LP relaxation.

The Mem(b) function used inside the memory constraint correctly reflects the quantized KV Cache footprint (accounting for asymmetric group-wise quantization with group size 128, per-token/per-channel layout, sequence length, batch size, and number of attention heads).
The optional bit-width set B used by the Integer Programming solver matches the per-model choices specified in Section 4.1.3.
Code has been implemented that uses the optional bit-width set B = {4, 8} when running block-wise memory allocation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B (Fbit = 4).

Code has been implemented that uses the optional bit-width set B = {2, 4} when running block-wise memory allocation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-70B, and QwQ-32B (Fbit = 2).
The memory budget M supplied to the Integer Program corresponds to the target GPU and batch-size configuration described in Section 4.1.3.

Code has been implemented that derives the KV Cache memory budget M from the target GPU capacity (e.g. 4090-24G, A100-40G, A100-80G), the model weight footprint, the batch size, and the maximum context length of 32,768 tokens.

Code has been implemented that supports two allocation regimes per model: the smaller batch size (e.g. BS=6 for LLaMA-8B, 32 for Qwen-7B, 12 for others) which forces mixed-precision, and the larger batch size which allows uniform Fbit — matching the pairs listed in Table 2.
The Integer Program is solved with CVXPY and returns a per-block Fbit assignment usable by the progressive quantization runtime.

Code has been implemented that expresses the objective and constraints using CVXPY primitives (cvxpy.Variable(..., boolean=True), cvxpy.Minimize, cvxpy.sum, and inequality constraints) and instantiates a cvxpy.Problem.
Code has been implemented that invokes Problem.solve() with a mixed-integer capable backend (e.g. GLPK_MI, CBC, or SCIP) and verifies the returned status is 'optimal'.
The CVXPY solve for the block-wise memory allocation IP completes within a few seconds (well under one minute) on the largest model considered (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-70B, 80 transformer blocks).

Code has been implemented that extracts the argmax of the solved x_{i,b} variables to produce a length-N integer list of Fbit values (one per transformer block) and serializes it to disk for downstream inference use.
The block-wise memory allocation is integrated into the PM-KVQ pipeline as specified in Section 3.4.
Code has been implemented that runs the sensitivity profiling and Integer Programming solve exactly once before inference begins, as the first stage of the pipeline described in Section 3.4.

Code has been implemented that passes the per-block Fbit assignment into the progressive quantization runtime so that each transformer block's KV Cache is shrunk to its assigned Fbit (rather than a uniform bit-width) once memory is saturated.
The measured outputs of block-wise memory allocation match the qualitative and quantitative claims made in Section 4.2 and Section 4.1.3.

For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on 1×4090-24G at BS=32, the solved allocation is a genuine mixed-precision (2/4-bit) assignment (not all-2-bit and not all-4-bit), matching the '2/4-2/4' label in Table 2.
For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B on 1×4090-24G at BS=6, the solved allocation is a genuine mixed-precision (4/8-bit) assignment, matching the '4/8-4/8' label in Table 2.

The total memory consumed by the resulting quantized KV Cache (across all transformer blocks) is strictly ≤ the budget M and typically exceeds the memory that a uniform lower-bit allocation would use, verifying that the solver actually fills the available memory.

For every evaluated model, transformer blocks with larger measured sensitivity s_{i,b} are assigned equal or higher bit-widths than blocks with smaller sensitivity by the IP solution (monotonicity check between sensitivity ranking and allocated Fbit).

Channel-wise reparameterization λ_i is calibrated via grid search over α∈[0,1] (grid size 20) on 512-token sequences, and positional interpolation with scaling factor s=4 is applied to embed 8192-token positional information into 2048-token calibration data via the modified RoPE rotary matrix; short-context calibration overhead is preserved.
Channel-wise reparameterization migrates Key-tensor outliers into the Query tensor before quantization, following the QServe-style formulation used in Equation (9) of Section 3.3.
Code has been implemented that defines a per-head, per-channel reparameterization vector λ (length d_head) attached to each attention block whose Key Cache is quantized.
Code has been implemented that applies K̃_i = K_i / λ_i to the Key tensor per channel and Q̃_i = Q_i · λ_i to the Query tensor per channel before the K tensor is passed to the quantizer.

The reparameterized attention path preserves Q̃K̃^T = QK^T to within floating-point tolerance when λ is applied and immediately inverted (unit test on a random batch confirms elementwise agreement with the unmodified attention logits before quantization).
Code has been implemented that stores the calibrated λ vector per attention block on disk (or in the model state) so it can be re-loaded at inference without re-running calibration.
λ_i is calibrated by grid-searching α∈[0,1] with grid size 20 on 512-token sequences, following Equation (10) and minimizing the self-attention reconstruction loss.
Code has been implemented that sweeps α over exactly 20 evenly spaced values in the closed interval [0, 1] during calibration of the reparameterization factor λ_i.

Code has been implemented that computes λ_i(α) from the token-position-indexed magnitudes of the Key and Query activations per Equation (10) (i.e. λ_i is a function of α and the per-channel statistics of |K_i| and |Q_i| aggregated over calibration tokens).

Code has been implemented that evaluates the reconstruction loss of the self-attention operator (e.g. MSE between the fp16 attention output and the reparameterized-plus-quantized attention output) as the objective the α grid search minimizes.
The grid search uses 512-token subsequences (drawn from the 2,048-token RedPajama calibration samples) as the input to the self-attention operator whose reconstruction loss is measured.
